To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the erythroctic glutathione levels of HIV patients are normal, but that the plasma levels of cysteine are elevated.
the erythrocity GSH levels are the same in healthy and HIV-infected subjects and that the Cys levels are supranormal in HIV-infected patients.
erythrocytic levels of GSH and GSSG are normal in HIV patients, whereas plasma Cys concentrations are supranormal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of glutathione and cysteine levels in HIV patients.
the determination of erythrocytic glutathione and plasma cysteine in HIV patients, using high performance liquid chromotography with dual electrochemcial detection.
the study of the redox status in human blood and its possible relation to HIV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV patients are normal with respect to erythrocytic levels of glutathion and cysteine, except for a subgroup with the most severe immunodeficiency and infections.
HIV-infected patients have normal erythrocysteine (ECys) and erythrocytic glutathione (EGSH) levels and that their erythrocytic cysteine levels are higher than those of healthy subjects.
the erythro-cylic GSH levels are normal in HIV patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the erythrolytic GSH status is a useful biomarker of HIV infection and its complications.
the HIV patients are in a state of oxidative stress.
HIV patients are not GSH deficient, although their Cys levels are higher than in healthy subjects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the erythrocellular GSH levels are not altered in HIV patients.
the GSH levels in erythrocytes are not a reliable indicator of the GSH levels of other cells in HIV patients.
HIV infection does not affect GSH levels, but it does increase Cys levels.
